title: The Sensory Dynamics of Coffee Extraction
content: Coffee extraction is a time-dependent physicochemical process in which constituents are released from a heterogeneous roasted matrix and transported into water. The sensory profile of the resulting beverage cannot be inferred from total dissolved solids or extraction yield alone, because individual compounds exhibit different extraction kinetics, chemical activities, and perceptual effects. This article develops a theoretical framework coupling particle-scale release, liquid-phase transport, beverage composition, volatile partitioning, and sensory response. A multicomponent mass-balance model is formulated for fast- and slow-accessible domains, with extensions for percolation flow, temperature dependence, volatile loss, and successive brew fractions. A separate perceptual layer represents attribute-specific concentration–response functions, mixture interactions, cross-modal aroma effects, and temporal adaptation. The framework distinguishes extraction time from sensory evaluation time and separates analytical concentration from perceived intensity and consumer liking. The model is not presented as experimentally validated; it establishes explicit assumptions, equations, limiting cases, and testable propositions. The analysis provides a mechanistic basis for interpreting why coffees with similar bulk extraction metrics may express different sensory profiles and why sensory attributes may evolve non-monotonically across brewing fractions.
